title: Allosteric activation of the glutamate receptor mGlu2 by the serotonin receptor 5-HT_2A

paper_content.abstract:
G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) dimers and higher-order oligomers are the subject of intense
debates. The complexes formed between two or more different GPCRs enable the cell to integrate
several signals. But the mechanisms of the allosteric interaction within these oligomers remain
unclear. Here, we use as a model the heteromer formed in the brain between two targets of anti-
psychotic drugs, the metabotropic glutamate receptor 2 (mGlu2) and the serotonin receptor 5-HT .
2A
Using molecular dynamics, a nanobody-based sensor and resonance energy transfer assays, we
demonstrate that the 5-HT receptor behaves as a positive allosteric modulator by stabilizing the
2A
active conformation of mGlu2. Using cysteine cross-linking experiments and mGlu2 sensors, we
reveal the molecular basis for this allosteric modulation of the mGlu2 receptor by 5-HT , an effect
2A
also mediated by other GPCRs. Our results thus provide insights into the allosteric control of a
GPCR activity via heteromerization with another receptor.
paper_content.introduction:
G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are the largest family of membrane proteins and are the
target of around 30% of marketed drugs1, 2. Upon activation by extracellular stimuli, they transduce
signals by coupling to heterotrimeric G protein proteins from different families3. Given that
individual cells express dozens of distinct GPCR subtypes, it raises the question of how the cells
integrate signals from such a diverse receptor repertoire. For over two decades, GPCR dimers and
higher-order oligomers were viewed as a possible way of signal integration (Fig. 1a)4-7, but this
subject raised intense debates8-10. Today, although such complexes are being considered, a more
accepted view is that different GPCRs can interact transiently11, 12, but the functional consequence
of such interaction remains more than elusive13-15. It is therefore important to understand how one
GPCR subtype regulates the function of another, as such knowledge may enable the development
of drugs that precisely tune GPCR signaling16.

The molecular mechanisms of allosteric interaction between GPCRs within these
oligomers, and in particular within heteromers formed of two different receptors6, are still unclear.
The molecular basis of direct interactions between GPCRs begins to be understood, thanks to
recent structural17-21 and biochemical13, 22 studies that have revealed possible dimerization
interfaces between receptors. Interestingly, homodimers can adopt an asymmetric interface in the
active state19, 20, consistent with the asymmetric functioning reported for many class A GPCR
dimers23-25, the most abundant receptors accounting for 90% of mammalian GPCRs. Class C
GPCRs19, 20, which classically form obligate dimers26, have also been studied in this regard. This
stands in contrast to class A receptors, for which the monomer has been demonstrated to be the
necessary and sufficient signaling unit27. In dimers and higher-order oligomers formed by class A
GPCRs, the seven transmembrane domains (7TMs) play a key role in stabilizing complexes, with
almost all TMs that could be involved in dimerization or oligomerization interfaces21. For dimeric
class C GPCRs, rearrangement of the dimerization interface during activation is well-characterized.
In the inactive state, the dimer interface is generally stabilized by interactions involving TM4 and
TM5 from each protomers22, 28, 29. A major reorientation of the dimer interface is observed during
agonist activation, where the two TM6s come into contact, a conserved conformation that enables
G protein coupling30. Recent structures of class C GPCRs also revealed the structural basis of the
asymmetry that occurs at the 7TM interface during G protein coupling19, 20. The rearrangement of
the 7TM interface for other GPCRs, such as class A receptors, is unclear, and some studies have
also proposed a relative repositioning of these transmembrane domains between the protomers31.

On the other hand, the molecular basis of allosteric interactions between two different
GPCRs in a heteromer remains poorly defined. Indeed, very few structures of complexes between
two different 7TMs have been solved, with the exception of the obligatory class C GABA
B
heterodimer28, 32, the sweet taste receptor33-35 and the recently discovered mGlu heterodimers29, 36,
37. Heterodimeric complexes formed between a class A GPCR and a class C GPCR are valuable
models for studying receptor heteromers, owing to both structural and physiological insights.
Firstly, the 7TM interfaces of several class C GPCR dimers in the inactive and active states has
recently been well characterized19, 20. Secondly, several heteromers formed between class C and
class A GPCRs have been shown to be physiologically relevant, including combinations between
several mGlu receptors and receptors of neurotransmitters (serotonin, dopamine or adenosine
receptors), including the mGlu2-5-HT 38 , mGlu5-D139 and mGlu5-A -D240 heteromers. Among
2A 2A
them, the properties of the mGlu2-5-HT heteromer have been extensively studied, as such
2A
heterocomplex has been proposed as an important target for antipsychotics38, 41-46. Nevertheless,
the structural basis for the allosteric control of the mGlu2 receptor by 5-HT remains elusive.
2A

In this study, we used the mGlu2-5-HT receptor complex as a model to examine the
2A
molecular basis of the allosteric interaction between a class A and a class C GPCR. This receptor
complex was first reported over fifteen years ago, and subsequent in vivo studies have confirmed
the negative synergy of the mGlu2 and 5-HT receptors during schizophrenia and antipsychotic
2A
treatment42, 47. For example, the antipsychotic effects of clozapine on the 5-HT receptor require
2A
the expression of mGlu2 receptor48. Furthermore, the activation of the mGlu2 receptor has been
proposed to promote the anti-dyskinetic and anti-psychotic effects of 5-HT in the treatment of
2A
Parkinson’s disease49. Through molecular modelling, resonance energy assays and cysteine
crosslinking, we demonstrate that 5-HT receptor behaves as a positive allosteric modulator,
2A
stabilizing the active conformation of mGlu2. Strikingly, we also find that this allosteric activation
of mGlu2 is not specifically mediated by 5-HT receptors, but also mediated by many other class
2A
A GPCRs, including the several dopamine and serotonin receptors. Collectively, our results
provide insights into the allosteric control of a GPCR activity through heteromerization.
paper_content.results:
Direct interaction between mGlu2 and 5-HT receptors at cell surface
2A
We first verified the interaction between mGlu2 and 5-HT receptors by time-resolved
2A
fluorescence resonance energy transfer (TR-FRET) saturation assays50. HEK-293 cells were co-
transfected with Snap-tagged mGlu2 (SmGlu2) and Halo-tag 5-HT (H5-HT ) for orthogonal
2A 2A
labeling of two receptors with non-cell permeant fluorescent substrates specific of these tags
attached to the extracellular N-terminal of each receptor. To minimize the difference in size of the
N-terminal region between mGlu2 receptor, which has a large extracellular domain (563 residues),
and 5-HT , which has a short N-terminal sequence (67 residues), the Halo-tag (33 kDa) and Snap-
2A
tag (21 kDa) were fused to the 5-HT and mGlu2 receptors respectively51. We also optimized the
2A
labelling conditions to obtain a strong FRET signal (Supplementary Fig. 1). Saturation curve
analysis showed a strong FRET signal between SmGlu2 and H5-HT (Fig. 1b and Supplementary
2A
Fig. 2), albeit lower than the FRET signal measured between the SmGlu2 and HmGlu2 subunits,
which form a constitutive homodimer26, 52. A strong FRET signal was also observed between
SmGlu2 and the Halo-tagged dopamine D1 receptor HD1 (N-terminal region of 20 residues)
(Supplementary Fig. 3). In contrast, a weak FRET signal was obtained between SmGlu2 and the
Halo-tagged M2 muscarinic receptor (HM2, this negative control containing 18 amino-acids in its
N-terminal region; Fig. 1b), as well as sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor 1 (HS1P1R, 41 amino-
acids in its N-terminal region; Supplementary Fig. 3). Notably, the FRET signal intensity did not
correlate with the N-terminal length of the class A GPCRs tested. These data demonstrate a strong
propensity for mGlu2 to form a complex with 5-HT , consistent with previous studies38, 42, 53.
2A

3D model of the mGlu2-5-HT complex
2A
Structures of the full-length mGlu2 receptor in the inactive and active states20, 29 revealed the
relative rearrangement of the transmembrane domain interface in the homodimer upon agonist
activation. In the inactive state, stabilized by a competitive antagonist bound into the glutamate
binding site and a negative modulator bound into a transmembrane domain of the homodimer, the
transmembrane interface is composed of TM4 and TM320 (Fig. 2a-b). In the active state, the two
TM6s form the homodimer interface20, 29 (Fig. 2c-d). These structural data are consistent with the
model of 7TM rearrangement we previously proposed based on cysteine cross-linking experiments
of the mGlu2 receptor expressed at the surface of living cells22. In our previous work, we showed
that the mGlu2 receptor in its active state can form a homo-oligomer via the TM4-TM5 interface.
This finding suggested that the mGlu2 receptor can form higher-order complexes with other
membrane proteins across this interface.

To investigate the heteromeric interface, we generated a realistic and unbiased 3D model of
the active mGlu2 homodimer in complex with the 5-HT receptor. As our study was carried out
2A
before the structures of the two receptors were available, thus an initial homology model was built
for the active mGlu2 homodimer, where the two protomers interact via a symmetrical TM5-TM6
interface, and the inactive 5-HT receptor. In all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of
2A
the isolated mGlu2 homodimer, the TM5-TM6 interface between the mGlu2 protomers
progressively decreases its contact surface on the intracellular side and rotates towards a TM6-
TM6 interface, which is maintained until the end of the simulation (Fig. 2e-f). Subsequently, a
heterodimeric mGlu2-5-HT complex between mGlu2 homodimer and a 5-HT monomer was
2A 2A
assembled by protein-protein docking, and an-unbiased molecular dynamics revealed a
symmetrical interface TM4-TM5 between the two receptors. During this simulation, we observed
that the conformation of mGlu2 promoters was stable in the mGlu2-5-HT complex, with RMSDs
2A
similar to those observed in the mGlu2 homodimer alone (average RMSD of 2.0 Å for the protomer
interacting with 5-HT and 1.8 Å for the other; Supplementary Fig. 4a). Similarly, the 5-HT
2A 2A
maintained initial inactive conformation was also stable throughout our MD simulations, either in
the mGlu2-5-HT complex or in monomeric form (average RMSDs of 2.0 Å and 2.1 Å,
2A
respectively, Supplementary Fig. 4b). Consequently, this initial model of the mGlu2-5-HT
2A
complex was deemed to be an appropriate tool for studying inter- and intra-receptor functional
effects and for guiding the subsequent cross-linking experiments. More recently, we have further
validated this model through a new complex model built from experimental structures, the cryo-
EM structures of the mGlu2 homodimer20 and 5-HT receptor54 (see Materials and Methods). To
2A
confirm their consistency, we submitted both models, based on homology modeling and on
experimental structures, to the same protocol of coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations
(CG MD; see Methods). This level of representation is well suited for comparing the organization
and persistence of pre-formed dimeric interfaces, as it allows access to longer effective simulation
timescales than would be feasible with all-atom models while retaining the key features of protein–
protein contacts. Because our analysis focused on the stability and similarity of existing interfaces
rather than on association/dissociation processes or detailed kinetics, standard coarse-grained MD
simulations were sufficient for this purpose, and no enhanced sampling methods were required. In
these CG trajectories, both models displayed the same general orientation of the protomers
(Supplementary Fig. 5a and 7e), with several common contacts at the interfaces
(Supplementary Fig. 5b and Fig. 7f). Moreover, the stability of the interfaces was preserved
across the CG MD trajectories (Supplementary Fig. 6d, 7d and 7e).

Cys cross-linking to characterize the mGlu2-5-HT complex
2A
We first validated this model of interaction between mGlu2 and 5-HT receptors with receptors
2A
expressed at the cell surface of HEK293 cells. First, we show that the mGlu2 agonist LY379268
increases the FRET signal between the two receptors when co-transfected (Fig. 3a and
Supplementary Fig. 8). This indicates that additional heteromers between these two receptors are
formed, although we cannot exclude that the increase in FRET signal results from a conformational
change between the two receptors (Supplementary Fig. 9a). In contrast, we verified that the
competitive antagonist LY341495 of mGlu2 did not alter the saturation curve (Supplementary
Fig. 9b). This is consistent with our model that only the mGlu2 receptor in the active conformation
can form a complex with the 5-HT receptor (Fig. 2e-f).
2A
Next, to further validate our model of the mGlu2-5-HT complex, we performed a
2A
cysteine disulfide crosslinking analysis. This technique probes proximity (< 8Å) between
engineered cysteine residues, enabling the detection of possible protein-protein interactions on the
cell surface. This approach has been successfully applied to study the dimeric 7TM interfaces of
several class C GPCRs, including the mGlu222 and calcium-sensing (CaS) receptor homodimers55,
the mGlu2-7 heterodimer29 and the GABA
B
receptor hetero-oligomer56. To detect the crosslinked
heterodimer in blots, Snap-tagged S5-HT and Halo-tagged HmGlu2 subunits were used to allow
2A
their specific labeling at the cell surface using non-cell permeant fluorescent substrates. This
allows direct fluorescence visualization of the receptors on blots, as previously reported22. Prior to
probing the heterodimeric interface, we first designed a mGlu2 mutant that stabilizes the active
state of mGlu2 in the absence of agonist. Based on our 3D model, the mGlu2Y6.58C mutation was
introduced into Halo-tagged wild-type mGlu2 (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Fig. 9c-d). This
construct, in which the active TM6-TM6 interface is stabilized by a disulfide bridge between the
two Cys6.58, was named “Active control” (mGlu2Ctrl) (Fig. 3b). We have shown that this mGlu2Ctrl
construct has a strong constitutive activity upon CuP treatment, which promotes disulfide
crosslinking, by measuring the constitutive accumulation of inositol phosphate-1 (IP ; 1
Supplementary Fig. 9e). To verify the presence of disulfide bridge crosslinking between the two
Cys6.58 in the mGlu2 homodimer in blot analysis, we used a construct in which the natural
intersubunit disulfide bridge through Cys121 was removed (Supplementary Fig. 9f), as it was
done previously22. A majority of mGlu2 dimers were observed after CuP treatment, an effect
reduced by an mGlu2 antagonist (Supplementary Fig. 9f). Overall, these results demonstrate that
Cys6.58 effectively stabilizes the active conformation of mGlu2 homodimer.
Next, to crosslink the HmGlu2Ctrl and S5-HT receptors (Fig. 3c-d), we introduced Cys at
2A
positions 5.42 and 5.41 in the HmGlu2Ctrl and S5-HT receptors, respectively, based on our 3D
2A
model (Supplementary Fig. 9c-d). We quantified on blots the S5-HT monomer (M), dimer (D)
2A
and S5-HT cross-linked to mGlu2 (mGlu2-5HT oligomers; O) thanks to the fluorescent Snap
2A 2A
substrates labelling. The efficiency of cross-linking between the two receptors induced by CuP
was quantified by the change of the ratio of the amounts for O/(M+D+O) before and after CuP
treatment. Interestingly, when co-expressing these two mutants, we obtained a CuP-induced high
molecular weight band (over 300 kDa) (Fig. 3e-f) that was suppressed by treatment with the
reducing agent DTT (Supplementary Fig. 10a-b). A similar band was obtained with wild-type
HmGlu2 containing a Cys in position 5.42, but the amount of cross-linked oligomer was clearly
increased in the presence of the mGlu2 agonist LY379268 (Fig. 3g-h). This shows the advantage
of using the HmGlu2Ctrl construct over wild-type HmGlu2 to study the heteromeric interface by
crosslinking since it does not require agonist treatment. Finally, the heteromeric composition of
this complex was confirmed by labeling the HmGlu2 and the S5-HT constructs with the
2A
fluorescent substrate Halo-Tag Alexa Fluor 660 and Snap-Surface Alexa Fluor 782, respectively
(Supplementary Fig. 10c-e). The high molecular weight band was visualized with both
fluorophores, confirming it contains both receptor subunits.
Our crosslinking analysis revealed that the heteromeric interface between HmGlu2 and
S5HT involves TM5 of both receptors, while a distinct disulfide bond between TM6 helices
2A
stabilizes the active conformation of the mGlu2 homodimer (Fig. 3d). Furthermore, our structural
model of the heterocomplex suggests a potential additional interaction interface involving the TM4
helices of both receptors (Fig. 2e-f). This possibility is supported by prior evidence implicating
TM4 in the oligomerization interface of active mGlu2 homodimers22. In contrast, the dimerization
interface of the 5-HT receptor is unclear57, and the experiments above indicate that only TM5 is
2A
involved (Fig. 3e-h). Therefore, we investigated the S5-HT homodimer interface by Cys
2A
crosslinking (Supplementary Fig. 11a), before further studying the mGlu2-5-HT interface.
2A
Symmetrical Cys crosslinking showed that TM4 of S5-HT was extensively crosslinked in the
2A
homodimer, in addition to TM5 and TM1 (Supplementary Fig. 11b-e). These results indicate that
5-HT can homodimerize across two possible symmetrical interfaces involving either TM4-TM5
2A
or TM1 (Supplementary Fig. 11d-e).
The above experiments indicate that TM4 of both mGlu2 and 5-HT receptors may be
2A
involved in their direct interactions. We then systematically mapped possible crosslinks involving
the TM4 and TM5 of these two receptors (Fig. 4a-b and Supplementary Fig. 12). Our data
showed that the greatest number of cross-links were obtained between TM5 of HmGlu2 and TM4
of S5-HT receptor (Fig. 4a-c and Supplementary Fig. 12). In contrast, no crosslinking was
2A
detected between mGlu2 and either TM1 or TM6 of the S5-HT receptor (Supplementary Fig.
2A
13a-b). These results show that TM4s and TM5s of mGlu2 and 5-HT receptors are primarily
2A
responsible for heteromer formation (Fig. 4d). This is highly consistent to previous findings that
Ala4.40, Ala4.44 and Ala4.48 located in mGlu2 TM4 are necessary for the mGlu2 to form a GPCR
complex with 5-HT receptor43, 46.
2A
In summary, our 3D models of the mGlu2-5-HT complex, together with crosslinking
2A
evidence, have strongly demonstrated that mGlu2 can interact directly with 5-HT to form a
2A
heteromer at the cell surface via their TM4-TM5 interface. Based on cross-linking results for the
5-HT homodimer, we cannot exclude that a 5-HT homodimer stabilized by TM1-TM1
2A 2A
interface is formed in the mGlu2-5-HT complex (Supplementary Fig. 14).
2A

5-HT stabilizes the mGlu2 receptor active state
2A
We used our recently developed nanobody-based FRET sensor58 to monitor the active
conformation of the mGlu2 receptor by detecting the active state of the extracellular glutamate
binding domain (Fig. 5a). This sensor is based on the measurement of a FRET signal between a
pair of fluorescent anti-mGlu2 nanobodies in the presence of LY379268 (Fig. 5a-b). The DN10
nanobody specifically binds the active conformation of the mGlu2 receptor favored by the agonist,
while the DN1 is not sensitive to the conformational state of the mGlu2 receptor58, 59. Interestingly,
the increase in transfected 5-HT receptor in the cell in the presence of a fixed amount of
2A
cotransfected mGlu2 receptor corresponded to an increase in FRET signal (Fig. 5b and
Supplementary Fig. 15), even in the absence of LY379268. This effect was prevented by the
mGlu2 antagonist (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. 15), but was not influenced by 5-HT
2A
agonist or antagonist (Fig. 5c). Altogether, these data demonstrate that 5-HT receptor, either in
2A
its inactive or active conformation, stabilizes the active conformation of the mGlu2 receptor. To
rule out the possibility that the DN10 nanobody is responsible for this increase in FRET by
stabilization of the active mGlu2 receptor, we monitored the conformational rearrangement of the
mGlu2 extracellular binding domain using our Snap-tagged mGlu2 sensor59-61. Consistent with the
nanobody-based FRET sensor results, the increase in transfected 5-HT receptor in the presence
2A
of a fixed amount of cotransfected mGlu2 receptor decreased TR-FRET ratio of SmGlu2 dimers
(Supplementary Fig. 16a, b) and increased in the proportion of the mGlu2 receptors in an active
state (Supplementary Fig. 16a, c). This effect occurs at lower concentration of 5-HT than when
2A
measured with the nanobody based assay, a difference that can be explained by the different timing,
the nanobody based assay being measured after overnight incubation with the nanobodies. Of
importance, this effect was not observed with the M2 receptor used as a negative control
(Supplementary Fig. 16d, e), since it does not have a tendency to interact directly to the mGlu2
receptor.
This conclusion is further supported by the behavior of a 5-HT receptor mutant (R173P)
2A
located in the intracellular part of TM3. This mutant is deficient in G protein coupling (Fig. 6a),
but it can still stabilize the active state of the mGlu2 receptor, as observed by the increased of
FRET signal (Fig. 5d). Of note, this 5-HT R173P mutant corresponds to the mutation of the Arg
2A
residue of the DRY motif that is highly conserved in class A GPCRs62, 63. Although mutation R173
into proline has not been reported to our knowledge in the 5-HT
2A
receptor, mutation of this residue
in other class A GPCRs strongly impairs G protein coupling63. Here, we show that R173P mutant
was expressed at the cell surface similarly to the wild-type (Supplementary Fig. 17a).
Furthermore, this mutation prevents the transactivation of 5-HT receptor by the LY379268
2A
activated mGlu2 receptor (Supplementary Fig. 17b-e), as measured by the intracellular calcium
release induced by mGlu2 in the presence of co-transfected 5-HT receptor44.
2A
We then confirmed the stabilization of the active state of mGlu2 receptor by 5-HT by
2A
measuring the accumulation of inositol phosphate-1 (IP ), using a chimeric Gqi protein to couple
1 9
mGlu2 to phospholipase C (PLC)22. The 5-HT R173P mutant increases the basal activity of the
2A
co-expressed mGlu2 receptor (Fig. 6b), which can be blocked by the competitive antagonist
LY341495 or a negative allosteric modulator that binds to the mGlu2 transmembrane domain22
(Fig. 6c). This increase in basal activity is rather modest, but it is significant. This finding is
consistent with other data above showing that 5-HT receptors stabilize only a fraction of the
2A
mGlu2 receptors in an active state (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. 15a). In addition, as expected
from a low fraction of the mGlu2 receptors interacting with the 5-HT R173P mutant, no
2A
significant increase of the potency of the mGlu2 agonist by co-expression of the 5-HT R173P
2A
mutant is observed (Supplementary Fig. 17f). Finally, a lower intracellular calcium mobilization
by the LY379268 activated mGlu2 receptor in presence of Gqi and the 5-HT R173P mutant is
9 2A
measured (Fig. 6d), and it is not related to the mGlu2 cell surface expression level
(Supplementary Fig. 17g). This observation supports the effect of this 5-HT mutant in
2A
increasing the basal activity of mGlu2 receptor by a direct interaction. Indeed, it is recognized that
a basal activation of PLC, such as that resulting from a GPCR constitutive activity, can partly
empty the intracellular calcium stores, leading to a decrease in the calcium signal induced by the
activation of a PLC-coupled GPCR.
Altogether, these data demonstrate that 5-HT
2A
acts as a positive allosteric modulator on
mGlu2 receptor activation even under basal conditions where only ambient glutamate may be
present64.

The mGlu2 receptor active state is stabilized by other class A GPCRs
In order to clarify which GPCRs could interact with mGlu2 receptor at the cell surface, we
performed a systematic analysis with 44 different class A GPCRs tagged at their N terminus with
a Snap-tag, as illustrated in Figure 7a. By using the mGlu2 nanobody-based FRET sensor, a
number of these GPCRs generated a high FRET signal between the two mGlu2 nanobodies that
selectively bind on the active mGlu2, when coexpressed with HA-tagged mGlu2 receptor,
including 5-HT , the dopamine D1 to D4 receptors, while others generated lower but significant
2A
signals, such as the 5-HT , the adrenergic  and the delta opioid receptors. All others did no
2B 1A
generate a signal significantly higher than the background, including the histamine H1 to H3
receptors and the muscarinic M2 to M4 receptors. This was not explained by differences in the
amount of the receptors at the cell surface (Supplementary Fig. 18a,b) and there is no link with
the N-terminal length of these class A GPCRs such as short N-terminus for D1 receptor made of
20 residues, until the long N-terminus of the cannabinoid CB1 receptor which is formed by 111
residues.
We found that the Gs-coupled D1 receptor, which has a strong tendency to stabilize the
active conformation of mGlu2 receptor (Fig. 7a), in an expression level dependent manner (Fig.
7b). Consistently with this stabilization, the D1 receptor increased the basal accumulation of IP
1
by the co-expressed mGlu2 receptor (Fig. 7c), an increase that was not observed when the D1
receptor was expressed alone. This basal activation of mGlu2 receptor by D1 receptor is also
supported by the lower calcium mobilization of the agonist-induced mGlu2 when D1 receptor is
coexpressed (Supplementary Fig. 18c) despite a similar expression of mGlu2 (Supplementary
Fig. 18d). As for 5-HT receptor, no significant increase of the potency of the mGlu2 agonist by
2A
co-expression of the D1 receptor is observed (Supplementary Fig. 18e), consistent with a low
fraction of the mGlu2 receptors interacting with the D1 receptor. Altogether, these data indicate
the effect of D1 receptor increases the constitutive activity of mGlu2 by a direct allosteric
interaction.
To further support the specific allosteric effect of both 5-HT and D1 receptors on mGlu2
2A
receptor, we used the Gi/o-coupled M2 receptor, one of the class A GPCRs that generated no
increase of FRET signal by the nanobody-based mGlu2 sensor (Fig. 7a). This is consistent with
the low FRET signal between the M2 and mGlu2 receptors shown above (Fig. 1b and
Supplementary Fig. 3) showing that the M2 receptor is less prone to interact with mGlu2 receptor
than 5-HT receptor. Increasing the M2 receptor versus mGlu2 receptor expression ratio did not
2A
result in an increase in the nanobody-based FRET sensor for mGlu2 activation (Fig. 7d).
Consistent with this absence of effect, a M2 mutant dead for the coupling to G protein (R121P also
mutated in the DRY motif; Supplementary Fig. 19a), did not increase the basal accumulation of
IP by the co-expressed mGlu2 receptor (Fig. 7e), despite its similar expression at the cell surface
1
compared to that of the wild-type M2 receptor (Supplementary Fig. 19b). Furthermore, this M2
R121P mutant did not alter the potency of the mGlu2 agonist in IP accumulation (Supplementary
1
Fig. 19c) and in the calcium responses (Supplementary Fig. 19d), despite a similar expression of
mGlu2 (Supplementary Fig. 19e).
Altogether, this demonstrates that mGlu2 receptor not only can be allosterically activated
by 5-HT receptor, but also by other class A GPCRs, even under basal conditions where only
2A
ambient glutamate may be present64.

Materials
LY379268, LY341495, MNI137, 5-HT (5-Hydroxytryptamine), Ketanserin tartrate were
purchased from Tocris Bioscience (Bristol, UK). Dichloro (1,10-phenanthroline) copper(II) (CuP)
were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA). Muscarine were purchased from
MedChemExpress (Shanghai, China). Lipofectamine 2000 was obtained from Thermo Fisher
Scientific (Carlsbad, CA, USA). Snap-Surface® Alexa Fluor® 782 was from New England
Biolabs. Halo-Tag® Alexa Fluor®660 and Coelenterazine-h were from Promega (Beijing) Biotech
Co. IP-One Gq kit, Snap-Green, Snap-Lumi4-Tb, Snap-Red, Halo-Green and Halo-Lumi4-Tb
were from Revvity Cisbio (Codolet, France), respectively.

Plasmids and transfection
The PRK5 plasmids encoding wild-type rat mGlu2, with HA and Snap or Flag and Halo inserted
just after the signal peptide were constructed as previously reported56. The plasmids encoding HA
and Snap or Flag and Halo tagged wild-type rat 5-HT were obtained in the same way. All the
2A
Cysteine mutants for mGlu2 and 5-HT together with G protein activation defective mutant 5-
2A
HT R173P and M2R121P were generated by site-directed mutagenesis using the QuikChange
2A
mutagenesis protocol (Agilent Technologies). All constructs were confirmed by DNA sequencing.
HEK293 cells (ATCC, CRL-1573, lot: 3449904) were cultured in DMEM (Gibco)
supplemented with 10% FBS (Gibco) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Gibco). For cross-linking
assay, HEK293 cells were transfected in 12 well plate with plasmids of interest by Lipofectamine
2000. For IP accumulation measurements, cells were transfected with the chimeric G-protein
1
Gqi9 and the glutamate transporter EAAC1 to enable mGlu2 receptor couple to the phospholipase
C pathway22.

20 ng of SmGlu2 plasmid cDNA and increasing amounts of HmGlu2, H5-HT or HM2R plasmid
2A
cDNA with 0, 5, 10, 20, 40, 60 and 80 ng, and completed to a total amount of 100 ng of plasmid

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This is a very elegant manuscript with a massive amount of work testing the residues of the 5-HT2A and mGlu2 receptors that mediate their physical interaction as a GPCR heterocomplex. The techniques involve TR-FRET, advanced computer modeling, cysteine crosslinking, and functional assays using both nanobody-based FRET and other traditional functional assays such as IP1. The authors propose an heteromeric interface between 5-HT2A and mGlu2 mediated via an asymmetric TM4-TM5 interaction, as well as a new allosteric interaction via which 5-HT2A modulates the G protein coupling preferences of the mGlu2 among Go vs Gi.
Comments:
The authors use non-cell permeant fluorescent substrates to test FRET (or molecular proximity between 5-HT2A and mGlu2). However, other groups have shown that 5-HT2A has a high level of basal endocytosis and intracellular localization (PMID: 18703670, PMID: 33082287, PMID:36795823). Does the use of non-cell permeant FRET substrates limit the population of 5-HT2A-mGlu2 complexes that is measured?
Can the authors provide a better explanation of the rationale behind the position of Halo-tag and Snap-tag? If the Halo-tag is located at the N-terminal of mGlu2, is the distance considering the large Venus flytrap extracellular domain of the class C GPCRs short enough to allow FRET with the Spap-tag located also at the N-terminal of the 5-HT2A? The authors mention this at the beginning of the results sections, but the effect of distance between the two N-terminals of mGlu2 and 5-HT2A is not clearly described.
Why the ratios of ExpH/ExpS in Fig 1 have a shorter range (less that 2) for the SmGlu2-H5-HT2A experiments, as compared to SmGlu2-HmGlu2 and SmGlu2-HM2R (above 3)?
Statistical analysis (comparing FRETmax and FRET50) are not assessed in the FRET saturation assays.
Authors show FRET signal using the “wild-type” 5-HT2A and mGlu2 receptors in Fig 1. This replicates what others have shown using assays in HEK293 cells under a “basal” state (i.e., without 5-HT2A or mGlu2 agonists) (PMID: 18297054, PMID: 19590495, PMID: 22300836; PMID: 29858599). However, the authors use a constitutively active mutant (mGlu2-Y6.58C, or mGlu2-Ctrl) to conduct all the very elegant cysteine-crosslinking studies. Have the authors tested cysteine-crosslinking with the “wild-type” mGlu2?
This is important because as mentioned (and demonstrated) by authors, the structural arrangement of the mGlu2 homodimer is changed upon agonist activation. Previous work by others indicates that TM4 (and in particular three alanine residues located at the intracellular half of the TM4 of the mGlu2: Ala4.40, Ala4.44 and Ala4.48) are necessary for the mGlu2 to form a GPCR complex with 5-HT2A (PMID: 23129762; PMID: 18297054; PMID: 37989895). This has been validated using photoactivatable unnatural amino acids (PMID: 32726588). How can the authors integrate their findings with a constitutively active mGlu2 mutant and previous findings using the wild-type mGluR2?
5-HT2A also forms homocomplexes (as shown by authors in Figure S4 and by others in PMID: 19279328). Would it be possible to model an alternative arrangement of the GPCR protomers in Fig 4D, showing proximity between the two 5-HT2A protomers?
As mentioned, the amount of work for the cysteine crosslinking assays is massive. However, it is not clear (in figure legends or methods) what signal is presented in the representative cross-linking studies. Did the authors use an immunoblot? If so, what antibody did the authors included? Was it targeting 5-HT2A or mGlu2? Again, this is not mentioned in methods, results or figure legends.
There is an always experimental variation in among all the SDS-PAGE gel electrophoresis experiments. However, authors present images coming from totally independent gels. This is not usually presented this way (PMID: 12496294, PMID: 16301531). How did the authors control for this inter-experimental variation?
Fig 5a - the cartoon on the left says “inactive” but has a LY379 bound to the Venus flytrap
Fig 5d – Is the buffer – mGlu2+5-HT2A-F173P condition different to the buffer – mGlu2 condition? This comparison is not shown in the figure panel.
For crosslinking assays in the presence of drugs, cells were incubated for 30 min, which may induce endocytosis. Was crosslinking observed at the cell surface or intracellularly?
Fig 3F – why the Y-axis goes from 0 to 30 if data are presented as %?
The authors elegantly show that 5-HT2A is able to recruit Gq signaling in cells expressing 5-HT2A alone (Fig S9c). Is has also been shown that LY379268-induced activation of mGlu2 trans-activates 5-HT2A and induces Gq dependent signaling (PMID: 29858599; PMID: 26758213). Does the 5-HT2A-F173P mutant prevent this trans-activation (i.e., effect of LY379268 on Gq signaling in cells co-expressing mGlu2 and 5-HT2A as compared to cells co-expressing mGlu2 and 5-HT2A-F173P)
The 3D model was carried out before the cryo-EM/X-ray structures of mGlu2 and 5-HT2A were available. How different is the 3D model using these new cryo-EM/X-ray structures?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The manuscript entitled “Allosteric activation of the glutamate receptor mGlu2 by the serotonin receptor 5-HT2A” (NCOMMS-25-07111) seeks to establish oligomerization of the mGlu2 homodimer with a class A GPCR, the serotonin receptor 2A (5-HT2A) as a mechanism for positive allosteric modulation of mGlu2. Initially, Gai et al. use FRET saturation experiments with N-terminally SNAP- and Halo-tagged receptors to prove the interaction of the aforementioned receptors within the plasma membrane of living cells. Again using resonance energy transfer experiments, they show that the dynamic equilibrium between active and inactive mGlu2 is shifted towards the active state in the presence of 5-HT2A, fostering the binding of an active state-specific nanobody. These effects were independent of 5-HT2A activation since incubation with 5-HT2A agonists or antagonists did not significantly alter the observed responses. In contrast, inhibition of mGlu2 with an antagonist reduces the interaction. Furthermore, the authors perform coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations with a homology model of the putative mGlu2/5-HT2A oligomer, leading to the identification of TMs4 and 5 being likely responsible for the protein-protein interaction. These computational studies inform cysteine-crosslinking experiments with engineered receptor mutants that the authors performed to identify individual residues of the involved receptors that are in close proximity to each other.
Although understanding how cells are able to integrate signals from multiple receptors is relevant, especially for complex structures such as the CNS, I cannot recommend the presented manuscript for publication in Nature Communications for the reasons detailed below:
Context and scientific rationale
• There is already a wealth of evidence for the direct interactions between mGlu2 and 5-HT2A in the literature. The manuscript only provides limited advancement to the field. This existing prior knowledge is not adequately reflected (in part not even mentioned):
Mutational studies and domain exchange analyses with mGlu3 already established TMs4 of both mGlu2 and 5-HT2A as most likely interacting domains, even specifying individual residues. The authors also do not comment on prior evidence on the mechanism for allosteric control of 5-HT2A signaling by mGlu2 (e.g. Moreno et al. J Biol Chem 287, 44301-44319, 2012 and Moreno et al. Sci. Signal. 9, ra5, 2016).
• What is the author’s rationale for using a labeling strategy (SNAP/Halo-tag) that only identifies receptors present on the cell surface, although it has been shown that the majority of 5-HT2A resides in intracellular compartments? It seems that the interaction of 5-HT2A and mGlu2 is a means for controlling mGlu2 surface expression (Toneatti et al. Sci. Signal. 13, eaaw3122, 2020).
• How do their results compare to previous evidence on hetero-oligomerization of these receptors acquired by BRET saturation and other techniques (e.g. Gonzales-Maeso et al., Nature, 2008, 93–97)?
• Likewise, it has already been shown that phosphorylation of a specific mGlu2 serine residue by 5-HT2A promotes Gi/o signaling (Murat et al. Mol Psychiatry 24, 1610–1626, 2019).
• On various occasions, the way scientific background is reported or data are interpreted makes it very complicated to understand the intention of the authors, especially for non-specialized readers. For example, in the introduction it is often unclear which specific homodimers they refer to or whether the authors discuss insights on class A or class C GPCRs, which differ dramatically in their overall architecture and function. Frequently, the authors write about “the two receptors” sometimes meaning to the two protomers of mGlu2 and on other occasions referring to the mGlu2-5-HT2A pair.
Description of the methodology
• The material and methods section lacks critical information that would be needed to reproduce the findings from the study. For example, neither cell densities, nor DNA amounts or at least relative ratios of the individual constructs used for transfections are indicated. How much protein was loaded on the individual blots? How was the protein concentration established? In general, all blots are cropped and missing loading controls.
• In nearly all Figures, normalized data is presented but there is no information on how normalization was performed.
• Although coarse-grained MD simulations are beyond the specific expertise of this reviewer, it must be stated that the description of the experimental procedure lacks critical details that are needed to fully understand or yet reproduce the authors’ experiments. For instance, there are no statements on how the authors dealt with the G proteins present in the cryo-EM structures used as templates, and neither did they comment on the large venus-fly trap domains present on mGlu2. Assuming that the G proteins were not part of the simulations, how did the authors ensure that their simulated “active states” were true active states without setting any constraints on the G protein-binding interfaces?
Technical aspects
• The authors use homology models for their MD simulations and saying that their study was initiated before high-resolution structures of mGlu2 and 5-HT2A were available. They state: “More recently, we have further validated this model through a new complex model built from the cryo-EM structures […]”. Is there any data supporting this claim?
• The authors use M2 as a negative control in their FRET saturation assays. Is there any evidence suggesting that this receptor does not interact with mGlu2? In fact, the FRET curve with M2 shows a nice saturation profile. The FRET signal is lower than with 5-HT2A but this could be an effect of different distances between the SNAP and Halo-tags, given that 5-HT2A has a much longer N-terminus (~68 AS) than M2 (~18AS). A more appropriate experiment to study the specificity of the interaction could be FRET competition assays with non-labeled 5-HT2A.
• Line 271: “Interestingly, the mGlu2 receptor activated by the 5-HT2A receptor can no longer induce Go protein rearrangement but can still induce Gi protein rearrangement.” - This conclusion is not valid. Once activated by an agonist, mGlu2 induces activation of Go, also in the presence of 5-HT2A. In contrast, there is a much smaller add-on effect of mGlu2 agonist on the signaling of Gi3 (Fig 6c).
• In Figure 1b, the authors draw a 2:1 stoichiometry of mGlu2 and 5-HT2A – could it also be 2:2 stoichiometry? Why is it drawn in 2:2 in Fig. 3d? In addition, there is a mistake in labeling: the Halo-tag of the high-FRET state (middle) does not glow, while in the low FRET state it glows (bottom).
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Gai and colleagues study mGlu2-5HT2a heterodimers using TR-FRET, oxidative crosslinking, modeling and BRET-based G protein activation assays. The main conclusion of the study is that 5HT2a acts as a positive allosteric modulator, capable of binding to and thus stabilizing the active conformation of the 7TM domains of mGlu2 dimers. Interestingly, the authors conclude that 5HT2a promotes mGlu2 activation of Gi but not Go heterotrimers, the latter being the predominant G protein expressed in neurons. While most of the data presented in the manuscript are consistent with this conclusion, the authors present little evidence that directly supports the model or rules out alternatives. There are also internal inconsistencies and conflicts with prior work that the authors do not address, as well as some technical shortcomings that undermine confidence in the work. In its present form the manuscript contains some interesting data but isn’t a complete and compelling report.
The strongest evidence supporting the authors’ model is shown in Figure 5b, which suggests that 5HT2a can drive mGlu2 towards the active state, apparently almost to the same extent as LY379268. The assay used here requires overnight incubation with ligands and nanobodies (Nb) at room temperature. As expression data are normalized there is no way to know if surface expression of mGlu2 changes as 5HT2a is increased, which could produce an increase in TR-FRET independent from receptor activation. Moreover, expression is said to be assessed using Tb emission after labeling of SNAP or Halo, therefore expression data presumably do not come from the same samples as the ones binding DN1-Tb. It is also unclear to what extent the assay is affected by the DN10 Nb itself, since this nanobody binds to the active state of the extracellular domain. This experiment is not controlled using another class A receptor that does not interact with mGlu2 and is described “triplicates from a typical experiment”, i.e. the results of one experiment. While intriguing, this result needs better controls and support from an orthogonal assay. One obvious alternative would be TR-FRET between SNAP and Halo tagged mGlu2 protomers, which the authors (and others) show is acutely sensitive to agonists and antagonists. This assay would allow the authors to combine expression of 5HT2a and real-time pharmacology using single samples.
Signaling studies using Gqi9 as a surrogate for Gi/o heterotrimers do not strongly support robust positive allosteric modulation of mGlu2 by 5HT2a. The enhancement due to 5HT2a F173P shown in Figure 5f is rather modest with n=3, and Figure S9a shows no change in the LY379268 EC50. The mGlu2/5HT2a expression ratio is not given here, mGlu2 surface expression is not quantified, and there is no negative control class A receptor.
BRET studies to assess heterotrimer activation show a large negative shift in the baseline when 5HT2a is expressed for Gi3 but not Go. The authors optimistically interpret this (in Figure 6b) as an increase in mGlu2-mediated activation of Gi3, but do not consider how this baseline shift can be much larger than the effect of a full agonist (Figure S10a). Since these assays are sensitive to overall expression of donors and acceptors it is much more likely that the baseline shift is an artifact of adding another overexpressed protein (5HT2a). Moreover, the agonist-induced BRET decrease for Gi3 is smaller in the presence of 5HT2a (Figure S10 and 6c) making it unclear if 5HT2a increases or decreases (or does not change) the ability of mGlu2 to activate Gi3. Clearly 5HT2a does not occlude Gi3 activation in this assay.
It is concerning that none of these BRET changes occur for GoB. The authors simply accept this at face value as evidence for 5HT2a-induced bias between closely-related G protein subtypes. Overall the BRET studies do not clearly support the authors’ model and indeed raise some doubts.
A large portion of the manuscript is devoted to “saturation” TR-FRET studies and oxidative crosslinking studies meant to provide evidence for the existence of mGlu2-5HT2a heterodimers and the relevance of a particular interprotomer interface. These studies are only tangentially related to the model the authors are proposing.
The crosslinking studies provide data that are consistent with the structural model, and the amount of work represented by these studies is appreciated. However, the results ultimately show that a TM4/5 interface for mGlu2 becomes accessible for crosslinking when this receptor is active, which could have been inferred from the already-available structures. The information gained here isn’t leveraged for functional studies. Again, the crosslinking studies aren’t controlled by any other class A GPCR.
Given the long history of this heterodimer (first described in 2008) the saturation TR-FRET studies cover old ground using methods with well-known technical limitations. A “saturating” curve is uninterpretable if acceptor density is normalized using donor density, and changes in response to agonist (as in Figure 3a) could reflect conformation as much as association. Agonist-induced changes are not controlled by any other TM protein. Here again there are unexplained inconsistencies. In the authors’ model some 5HT2a interacts with unliganded mGlu2 because of constitutive activity or ambient glutamate. Why then does agonist apparently enhance “association” with 5HT2a (Fig. 3a), but antagonist does not do the opposite (S2b).
The functional studies rely on a defective 5HT2a mutant F173P, which is described as a mutation in the intracellular part of TM3 that blocks G protein coupling. The rat 5HT2a sequence has no F residues in the intracellular part of TM3, and residue 173 is the R in the middle of the DRY motif. No citation is provided for whatever this mutant is, and the methods section on plasmid construction is also unhelpful. When used it is not clear than this mutant receptor was expressed at the cell surface, and validation for loss of function is minimal. It is not clear that Gqi9 is present in Figure 5e, which is necessary to interpret Figure 5F.
Throughout the manuscript there are instances of questionable experimental rigor. For example, in Figure 1 we are told “Data are means ± SEM of triplicates from a typical experiment”, which suggests three technical and one biological replicate. Similar descriptions appear in Figures 3a, 5b, S2, etc.. The legend for Figure 6b says 3 independent experiments but there are 10-12 data points on the bars, suggesting the authors are plotting technical replicates. Since an ANOVA is performed on these data it’s not clear what they are including. In Fig. 6c there are 6 points on the graph for “a typical experiment performed at least 3 times”.
This heteromeric complex has been studied for almost 20 years but the authors provide scant discussion to place their findings in context of what is already known. For example, how can these observations be reconciled with a report that mGlu2-dependent activation of Gi/o is unchanged in 5HT2a -/- mice (PMID: 26758213).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors have addressed all my previous comments except one: the potential role of residues Ala4.40, Ala4.44, and Ala4.48 in mGluR2 heteromerization with 5-HT2A. This point is important to evaluate the validity and replicability of their findings, as it has been reported by several independent groups (PMID: 23129762; PMID: 37989895).
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
I am happy that the authors have addressed most of my comments with their revised version of the manuscript “Allosteric activation of the glutamate receptor mGlu2 by the serotonin receptor 5-HT2A”.
I have one remaining query that relates to my original comment on the missing comparison of the 5-HT2A-mGlu2 homology model with the model built on the available high-resolution structures of the individual receptors:
While the authors now provide an overlay (in top view) of the simulation results from their homology model and the model obtained from experimental data, their conclusions on this comparison do not seem convincing. The new Supplementary Figure 5 shows obvious differences in the positioning of transmembrane helices 4 (and 5) of the 5-HT2AR relative to the mGlu2 protomers, a fact that the authors themselves admit within their experimental section:
“One difference between the two models is the position of TM4 of the 5-HT2A receptor. In homology model, this helix is located between TM5 of one mGlu2 protomer and TM6 of the other protomer. While in the new model, 5-HT2A TM4 moves towards to the TM5 of mGlu2 protomer, which explains the higher number of frequent contacts between mGlu2 TM5 and 5-HT2A TM4 observed in this case (Supplementary Fig. 7-8).”
In their main text and their point-by-point reply, however, they conclude: “Both displayed the same general orientation of the protomers (Supplementary Fig. 5a), with several common contacts at the interfaces (Supplementary Fig. 5b).”/ “It shows that the relative orientation of the protomers is the same in the two models, with a common mGlu2-5-HT2A interface.”
First, an additional view from the side could allow the reader to better assess the major differences in the conformations along helices 4 and 5 of 5-HT2AR. Second, in their point-by-point reply, Supplementary Fig. 5b is said to provide “the full lists of contact frequencies for both models”. However, this Figure only contains a list of amino acids labeled as “frequently observed in CGMD simulations of both heterotrimer models”, with no information on how “contacts” were defined, and what is meant by “frequently”. What were the additional contacts with the model derived from the experimental structures? Furthermore, what is the basis of the order of amino acids in this list? Third, while contact residues for the new model are highlighted in Supplementary Fig. 7e (although hardly visible), there is no data that allows comparison of the contacts between the two models. Unfortunately, the mentioned Supplementary Figure 8 shows something completely different (TR-FRET saturation analysis). The analysis of the “torsion angles” is not convincing either, as the interface appears to be located in the upper parts of 5-HT2AR. Are changes in these upper parts of the helices (e.g., tilting) expected to be captured by the derived torsion angle, given the position of the angle measurement at the bottom of the 5-HT2AR?
Moreover, while the authors mention in their rebuttal that they have provided uncropped gels/blots to allow further assessment of their cross-linking analyses within a Supplementary Data file, there actually is no such file within the documents shared for revision.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4: I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_5:
In this revised study, the authors propose a heteromeric interface between 5-HT₂A and mGlu2 mediated by TM4–TM5 interaction and identify a novel allosteric mechanism through which the 5-HT₂A receptor modulates mGlu2 signaling. This conclusion is supported by an integrated approach combining TR-FRET, advanced computational modeling, cysteine crosslinking, and functional assays. While previous studies have examined the interaction between mGlu2 and 5-HT₂A, this work provides an elegant and mechanistically detailed advance, supporting how a class A GPCR can allosterically modulate mGlu2 dimer signaling through specific transmembrane interactions. The experiments are generally well controlled, leveraging the availability of existing tools and methods, and I believe that the authors have adequately addressed prior reviewers’ concerns by providing additional supporting data and reasonable explanations in their rebuttal. I have minor recommendations, which are outlined below.
Specifics:
Because allosteric modulation is probe-dependent, one would expect the FRET response of the mGlu2–5-HT2A complex to differ when agonists other than LY379268 are used. Was this assessed? In addition, how does increasing the expression of unlabeled 5-HT2A affect the intramolecular FRET signal of mGlu2 dimers? Such an effect would be anticipated, as the presence of 5-HT2A is expected to allosterically modulate mGlu2 dimer conformation and signaling . If these data have already been obtained, they should be explicitly mentioned and discussed, as they would substantiate the claims put forth.
Suppl. Fig 5: It would be informative to provide the frequency (in percentage) for the common contact residues from TM4-TM5 of mGlu2 and 5-HT2A frequently observed in CGMD simulations.
Line 198: “We quantified on blots the S5-HT2A monomer (M), dimer (D)198and S5-HT2A cross-linked to mGlu2 (mGlu2-5HT2A oligomers; O)…” this nomenclature should also be used in the figure.
Line 226: “The above experiments indicate that TM4 of both receptors…” The description here lacks clarity regarding which receptors and complexes are being referred to. The authors should be more precise through the text (also mentioned in previous critics) in specifying whether these conclusions pertain to 5-HT2A–5-HT2A homomers or to the mGlu2–5-HT2A heteromer. This ambiguity is particularly confusing because the preceding results appear to describe 5-HT2A–5-HT2A interactions, whereas the subsequent experiment examines the mGlu2–5-HT2A complex. Clear and consistent identification of the receptor complexes under study is needed throughout the manuscript.
Line 269: The authors must mean Suppl. Fig 17b-e.
In general, I recommend that the authors carefully revise the manuscript, potentially with editorial assistance, to improve clarity, flow, and consistency of tense, particularly in the Introduction. I highlight only a few representative examples from the Introduction; similar issues are also evident in the newly added text.
“It is then of much interest to understand how one GPCR subtype can regulate the function of another ,as such information may be of interest to develop new drugs that precisely tune GPCR signaling.” I would suggest instead: It is therefore important to understand how one GPCR subtype regulates the function of another, as such knowledge may enable the development of drugs that precisely tune GPCR signaling?
“In contrast, a weak FRET signal was obtained between SmGlu2 and the Halo-tagged M2 muscarinic receptor(N-terminal region of 18 residues), the HM2 construct used a negative control (Fig. 1b); and also sphingosine-1 phosphate receptor 1 (N-terminal region of 41 residues), the construct HS1P1122 (Supplementary Fig. 3).” The syntax and punctuation are odd.
“It has also been studied for class C GPCRs, which classically form mandatory dimers, unlike all the other GPCRs, such as class A receptors, for which it has been demonstrated that the necessary and sufficient signaling unit is monomer”.
Ambiguous sentence…What has been studied? Please consider rephrasing.

## Abstract

G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) dimers and higher-order oligomers are the subject of intense
debates. The complexes formed between two or more different GPCRs enable the cell to integrate
several signals. But the mechanisms of the allosteric interaction within these oligomers remain
unclear. Here, we use as a model the heteromer formed in the brain between two targets of anti-
psychotic drugs, the metabotropic glutamate receptor 2 (mGlu2) and the serotonin receptor 5-HT .
2A
Using molecular dynamics, a nanobody-based sensor and resonance energy transfer assays, we
demonstrate that the 5-HT receptor behaves as a positive allosteric modulator by stabilizing the
2A
active conformation of mGlu2. Using cysteine cross-linking experiments and mGlu2 sensors, we
reveal the molecular basis for this allosteric modulation of the mGlu2 receptor by 5-HT , an effect
2A
also mediated by other GPCRs. Our results thus provide insights into the allosteric control of a
GPCR activity via heteromerization with another receptor.

---

## Introduction

G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are the largest family of membrane proteins and are the
target of around 30% of marketed drugs1, 2. Upon activation by extracellular stimuli, they transduce
signals by coupling to heterotrimeric G protein proteins from different families3. Given that
individual cells express dozens of distinct GPCR subtypes, it raises the question of how the cells
integrate signals from such a diverse receptor repertoire. For over two decades, GPCR dimers and
higher-order oligomers were viewed as a possible way of signal integration (Fig. 1a)4-7, but this
subject raised intense debates8-10. Today, although such complexes are being considered, a more
accepted view is that different GPCRs can interact transiently11, 12, but the functional consequence
of such interaction remains more than elusive13-15. It is therefore important to understand how one
GPCR subtype regulates the function of another, as such knowledge may enable the development
of drugs that precisely tune GPCR signaling16.

The molecular mechanisms of allosteric interaction between GPCRs within these
oligomers, and in particular within heteromers formed of two different receptors6, are still unclear.
The molecular basis of direct interactions between GPCRs begins to be understood, thanks to
recent structural17-21 and biochemical13, 22 studies that have revealed possible dimerization
interfaces between receptors. Interestingly, homodimers can adopt an asymmetric interface in the
active state19, 20, consistent with the asymmetric functioning reported for many class A GPCR
dimers23-25, the most abundant receptors accounting for 90% of mammalian GPCRs. Class C
GPCRs19, 20, which classically form obligate dimers26, have also been studied in this regard. This
stands in contrast to class A receptors, for which the monomer has been demonstrated to be the
necessary and sufficient signaling unit27. In dimers and higher-order oligomers formed by class A
GPCRs, the seven transmembrane domains (7TMs) play a key role in stabilizing complexes, with
almost all TMs that could be involved in dimerization or oligomerization interfaces21. For dimeric
class C GPCRs, rearrangement of the dimerization interface during activation is well-characterized.
In the inactive state, the dimer interface is generally stabilized by interactions involving TM4 and
TM5 from each protomers22, 28, 29. A major reorientation of the dimer interface is observed during
agonist activation, where the two TM6s come into contact, a conserved conformation that enables
G protein coupling30. Recent structures of class C GPCRs also revealed the structural basis of the
asymmetry that occurs at the 7TM interface during G protein coupling19, 20. The rearrangement of
the 7TM interface for other GPCRs, such as class A receptors, is unclear, and some studies have
also proposed a relative repositioning of these transmembrane domains between the protomers31.

On the other hand, the molecular basis of allosteric interactions between two different
GPCRs in a heteromer remains poorly defined. Indeed, very few structures of complexes between
two different 7TMs have been solved, with the exception of the obligatory class C GABA
B
heterodimer28, 32, the sweet taste receptor33-35 and the recently discovered mGlu heterodimers29, 36,
37. Heterodimeric complexes formed between a class A GPCR and a class C GPCR are valuable
models for studying receptor heteromers, owing to both structural and physiological insights.
Firstly, the 7TM interfaces of several class C GPCR dimers in the inactive and active states has
recently been well characterized19, 20. Secondly, several heteromers formed between class C and
class A GPCRs have been shown to be physiologically relevant, including combinations between
several mGlu receptors and receptors of neurotransmitters (serotonin, dopamine or adenosine
receptors), including the mGlu2-5-HT 38 , mGlu5-D139 and mGlu5-A -D240 heteromers. Among
2A 2A
them, the properties of the mGlu2-5-HT heteromer have been extensively studied, as such
2A
heterocomplex has been proposed as an important target for antipsychotics38, 41-46. Nevertheless,
the structural basis for the allosteric control of the mGlu2 receptor by 5-HT remains elusive.
2A

In this study, we used the mGlu2-5-HT receptor complex as a model to examine the
2A
molecular basis of the allosteric interaction between a class A and a class C GPCR. This receptor
complex was first reported over fifteen years ago, and subsequent in vivo studies have confirmed
the negative synergy of the mGlu2 and 5-HT receptors during schizophrenia and antipsychotic
2A
treatment42, 47. For example, the antipsychotic effects of clozapine on the 5-HT receptor require
2A
the expression of mGlu2 receptor48. Furthermore, the activation of the mGlu2 receptor has been
proposed to promote the anti-dyskinetic and anti-psychotic effects of 5-HT in the treatment of
2A
Parkinson’s disease49. Through molecular modelling, resonance energy assays and cysteine
crosslinking, we demonstrate that 5-HT receptor behaves as a positive allosteric modulator,
2A
stabilizing the active conformation of mGlu2. Strikingly, we also find that this allosteric activation
of mGlu2 is not specifically mediated by 5-HT receptors, but also mediated by many other class
2A
A GPCRs, including the several dopamine and serotonin receptors. Collectively, our results
provide insights into the allosteric control of a GPCR activity through heteromerization.

---

## Results

Direct interaction between mGlu2 and 5-HT receptors at cell surface
2A
We first verified the interaction between mGlu2 and 5-HT receptors by time-resolved
2A
fluorescence resonance energy transfer (TR-FRET) saturation assays50. HEK-293 cells were co-
transfected with Snap-tagged mGlu2 (SmGlu2) and Halo-tag 5-HT (H5-HT ) for orthogonal
2A 2A
labeling of two receptors with non-cell permeant fluorescent substrates specific of these tags
attached to the extracellular N-terminal of each receptor. To minimize the difference in size of the
N-terminal region between mGlu2 receptor, which has a large extracellular domain (563 residues),
and 5-HT , which has a short N-terminal sequence (67 residues), the Halo-tag (33 kDa) and Snap-
2A
tag (21 kDa) were fused to the 5-HT and mGlu2 receptors respectively51. We also optimized the
2A
labelling conditions to obtain a strong FRET signal (Supplementary Fig. 1). Saturation curve
analysis showed a strong FRET signal between SmGlu2 and H5-HT (Fig. 1b and Supplementary
2A
Fig. 2), albeit lower than the FRET signal measured between the SmGlu2 and HmGlu2 subunits,
which form a constitutive homodimer26, 52. A strong FRET signal was also observed between
SmGlu2 and the Halo-tagged dopamine D1 receptor HD1 (N-terminal region of 20 residues)
(Supplementary Fig. 3). In contrast, a weak FRET signal was obtained between SmGlu2 and the
Halo-tagged M2 muscarinic receptor (HM2, this negative control containing 18 amino-acids in its
N-terminal region; Fig. 1b), as well as sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor 1 (HS1P1R, 41 amino-
acids in its N-terminal region; Supplementary Fig. 3). Notably, the FRET signal intensity did not
correlate with the N-terminal length of the class A GPCRs tested. These data demonstrate a strong
propensity for mGlu2 to form a complex with 5-HT , consistent with previous studies38, 42, 53.
2A

3D model of the mGlu2-5-HT complex
2A
Structures of the full-length mGlu2 receptor in the inactive and active states20, 29 revealed the
relative rearrangement of the transmembrane domain interface in the homodimer upon agonist
activation. In the inactive state, stabilized by a competitive antagonist bound into the glutamate
binding site and a negative modulator bound into a transmembrane domain of the homodimer, the
transmembrane interface is composed of TM4 and TM320 (Fig. 2a-b). In the active state, the two
TM6s form the homodimer interface20, 29 (Fig. 2c-d). These structural data are consistent with the
model of 7TM rearrangement we previously proposed based on cysteine cross-linking experiments
of the mGlu2 receptor expressed at the surface of living cells22. In our previous work, we showed
that the mGlu2 receptor in its active state can form a homo-oligomer via the TM4-TM5 interface.
This finding suggested that the mGlu2 receptor can form higher-order complexes with other
membrane proteins across this interface.

To investigate the heteromeric interface, we generated a realistic and unbiased 3D model of
the active mGlu2 homodimer in complex with the 5-HT receptor. As our study was carried out
2A
before the structures of the two receptors were available, thus an initial homology model was built
for the active mGlu2 homodimer, where the two protomers interact via a symmetrical TM5-TM6
interface, and the inactive 5-HT receptor. In all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of
2A
the isolated mGlu2 homodimer, the TM5-TM6 interface between the mGlu2 protomers
progressively decreases its contact surface on the intracellular side and rotates towards a TM6-
TM6 interface, which is maintained until the end of the simulation (Fig. 2e-f). Subsequently, a
heterodimeric mGlu2-5-HT complex between mGlu2 homodimer and a 5-HT monomer was
2A 2A
assembled by protein-protein docking, and an-unbiased molecular dynamics revealed a
symmetrical interface TM4-TM5 between the two receptors. During this simulation, we observed
that the conformation of mGlu2 promoters was stable in the mGlu2-5-HT complex, with RMSDs
2A
similar to those observed in the mGlu2 homodimer alone (average RMSD of 2.0 Å for the protomer
interacting with 5-HT and 1.8 Å for the other; Supplementary Fig. 4a). Similarly, the 5-HT
2A 2A
maintained initial inactive conformation was also stable throughout our MD simulations, either in
the mGlu2-5-HT complex or in monomeric form (average RMSDs of 2.0 Å and 2.1 Å,
2A
respectively, Supplementary Fig. 4b). Consequently, this initial model of the mGlu2-5-HT
2A
complex was deemed to be an appropriate tool for studying inter- and intra-receptor functional
effects and for guiding the subsequent cross-linking experiments. More recently, we have further
validated this model through a new complex model built from experimental structures, the cryo-
EM structures of the mGlu2 homodimer20 and 5-HT receptor54 (see Materials and Methods). To
2A
confirm their consistency, we submitted both models, based on homology modeling and on
experimental structures, to the same protocol of coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations
(CG MD; see Methods). This level of representation is well suited for comparing the organization
and persistence of pre-formed dimeric interfaces, as it allows access to longer effective simulation
timescales than would be feasible with all-atom models while retaining the key features of protein–
protein contacts. Because our analysis focused on the stability and similarity of existing interfaces
rather than on association/dissociation processes or detailed kinetics, standard coarse-grained MD
simulations were sufficient for this purpose, and no enhanced sampling methods were required. In
these CG trajectories, both models displayed the same general orientation of the protomers
(Supplementary Fig. 5a and 7e), with several common contacts at the interfaces
(Supplementary Fig. 5b and Fig. 7f). Moreover, the stability of the interfaces was preserved
across the CG MD trajectories (Supplementary Fig. 6d, 7d and 7e).

Cys cross-linking to characterize the mGlu2-5-HT complex
2A
We first validated this model of interaction between mGlu2 and 5-HT receptors with receptors
2A
expressed at the cell surface of HEK293 cells. First, we show that the mGlu2 agonist LY379268
increases the FRET signal between the two receptors when co-transfected (Fig. 3a and
Supplementary Fig. 8). This indicates that additional heteromers between these two receptors are
formed, although we cannot exclude that the increase in FRET signal results from a conformational
change between the two receptors (Supplementary Fig. 9a). In contrast, we verified that the
competitive antagonist LY341495 of mGlu2 did not alter the saturation curve (Supplementary
Fig. 9b). This is consistent with our model that only the mGlu2 receptor in the active conformation
can form a complex with the 5-HT receptor (Fig. 2e-f).
2A
Next, to further validate our model of the mGlu2-5-HT complex, we performed a
2A
cysteine disulfide crosslinking analysis. This technique probes proximity (< 8Å) between
engineered cysteine residues, enabling the detection of possible protein-protein interactions on the
cell surface. This approach has been successfully applied to study the dimeric 7TM interfaces of
several class C GPCRs, including the mGlu222 and calcium-sensing (CaS) receptor homodimers55,
the mGlu2-7 heterodimer29 and the GABA
B
receptor hetero-oligomer56. To detect the crosslinked
heterodimer in blots, Snap-tagged S5-HT and Halo-tagged HmGlu2 subunits were used to allow
2A
their specific labeling at the cell surface using non-cell permeant fluorescent substrates. This
allows direct fluorescence visualization of the receptors on blots, as previously reported22. Prior to
probing the heterodimeric interface, we first designed a mGlu2 mutant that stabilizes the active
state of mGlu2 in the absence of agonist. Based on our 3D model, the mGlu2Y6.58C mutation was
introduced into Halo-tagged wild-type mGlu2 (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Fig. 9c-d). This
construct, in which the active TM6-TM6 interface is stabilized by a disulfide bridge between the

construct has a strong constitutive activity upon CuP treatment, which promotes disulfide
crosslinking, by measuring the constitutive accumulation of inositol phosphate-1 (IP ; 1
Supplementary Fig. 9e). To verify the presence of disulfide bridge crosslinking between the two

intersubunit disulfide bridge through Cys121 was removed (Supplementary Fig. 9f), as it was
done previously22. A majority of mGlu2 dimers were observed after CuP treatment, an effect

Cys6.58 effectively stabilizes the active conformation of mGlu2 homodimer.
Next, to crosslink the HmGlu2Ctrl and S5-HT receptors (Fig. 3c-d), we introduced Cys at
2A
positions 5.42 and 5.41 in the HmGlu2Ctrl and S5-HT receptors, respectively, based on our 3D
2A
model (Supplementary Fig. 9c-d). We quantified on blots the S5-HT monomer (M), dimer (D)
2A
and S5-HT cross-linked to mGlu2 (mGlu2-5HT oligomers; O) thanks to the fluorescent Snap
2A 2A
substrates labelling. The efficiency of cross-linking between the two receptors induced by CuP
was quantified by the change of the ratio of the amounts for O/(M+D+O) before and after CuP
treatment. Interestingly, when co-expressing these two mutants, we obtained a CuP-induced high
molecular weight band (over 300 kDa) (Fig. 3e-f) that was suppressed by treatment with the
reducing agent DTT (Supplementary Fig. 10a-b). A similar band was obtained with wild-type
HmGlu2 containing a Cys in position 5.42, but the amount of cross-linked oligomer was clearly
increased in the presence of the mGlu2 agonist LY379268 (Fig. 3g-h). This shows the advantage

crosslinking since it does not require agonist treatment. Finally, the heteromeric composition of
this complex was confirmed by labeling the HmGlu2 and the S5-HT constructs with the
2A
fluorescent substrate Halo-Tag Alexa Fluor 660 and Snap-Surface Alexa Fluor 782, respectively
(Supplementary Fig. 10c-e). The high molecular weight band was visualized with both
fluorophores, confirming it contains both receptor subunits.

S5HT involves TM5 of both receptors, while a distinct disulfide bond between TM6 helices
2A
stabilizes the active conformation of the mGlu2 homodimer (Fig. 3d). Furthermore, our structural
model of the heterocomplex suggests a potential additional interaction interface involving the TM4
helices of both receptors (Fig. 2e-f). This possibility is supported by prior evidence implicating

interface of the 5-HT receptor is unclear57, and the experiments above indicate that only TM5 is
2A
involved (Fig. 3e-h). Therefore, we investigated the S5-HT homodimer interface by Cys
2A
crosslinking (Supplementary Fig. 11a), before further studying the mGlu2-5-HT interface.
2A

2A
homodimer, in addition to TM5 and TM1 (Supplementary Fig. 11b-e). These results indicate that
5-HT can homodimerize across two possible symmetrical interfaces involving either TM4-TM5
2A
or TM1 (Supplementary Fig. 11d-e).

involved in their direct interactions. We then systematically mapped possible crosslinks involving
the TM4 and TM5 of these two receptors (Fig. 4a-b and Supplementary Fig. 12). Our data
showed that the greatest number of cross-links were obtained between TM5 of HmGlu2 and TM4
of S5-HT receptor (Fig. 4a-c and Supplementary Fig. 12). In contrast, no crosslinking was
2A
detected between mGlu2 and either TM1 or TM6 of the S5-HT receptor (Supplementary Fig.
2A
13a-b). These results show that TM4s and TM5s of mGlu2 and 5-HT receptors are primarily

5-HT homodimer, we cannot exclude that a 5-HT homodimer stabilized by TM1-TM1

interface is formed in the mGlu2-5-HT complex (Supplementary Fig. 14).
2A

while the DN1 is not sensitive to the conformational state of the mGlu2 receptor58, 59. Interestingly,
the increase in transfected 5-HT receptor in the cell in the presence of a fixed amount of
2A
cotransfected mGlu2 receptor corresponded to an increase in FRET signal (Fig. 5b and
Supplementary Fig. 15), even in the absence of LY379268. This effect was prevented by the
mGlu2 antagonist (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. 15), but was not influenced by 5-HT
2A
agonist or antagonist (Fig. 5c). Altogether, these data demonstrate that 5-HT receptor, either in
2A
its inactive or active conformation, stabilizes the active conformation of the mGlu2 receptor. To
rule out the possibility that the DN10 nanobody is responsible for this increase in FRET by
stabilization of the active mGlu2 receptor, we monitored the conformational rearrangement of the
mGlu2 extracellular binding domain using our Snap-tagged mGlu2 sensor59-61. Consistent with the
nanobody-based FRET sensor results, the increase in transfected 5-HT receptor in the presence
2A
of a fixed amount of cotransfected mGlu2 receptor decreased TR-FRET ratio of SmGlu2 dimers
(Supplementary Fig. 16a, b) and increased in the proportion of the mGlu2 receptors in an active
state (Supplementary Fig. 16a, c). This effect occurs at lower concentration of 5-HT than when
2A
measured with the nanobody based assay, a difference that can be explained by the different timing,
the nanobody based assay being measured after overnight incubation with the nanobodies. Of

located in the intracellular part of TM3. This mutant is deficient in G protein coupling (Fig. 6a),

2A
residue of the DRY motif that is highly conserved in class A GPCRs62, 63. Although mutation R173

We then confirmed the stabilization of the active state of mGlu2 receptor by 5-HT by
2A

(Fig. 6c). This increase in basal activity is rather modest, but it is significant. This finding is
consistent with other data above showing that 5-HT receptors stabilize only a fraction of the
2A
mGlu2 receptors in an active state (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. 15a). In addition, as expected

2A

2A
mutant is observed (Supplementary Fig. 17f). Finally, a lower intracellular calcium mobilization
by the LY379268 activated mGlu2 receptor in presence of Gqi and the 5-HT R173P mutant is
9 2A
measured (Fig. 6d), and it is not related to the mGlu2 cell surface expression level
(Supplementary Fig. 17g). This observation supports the effect of this 5-HT mutant in
2A

activation of a PLC-coupled GPCR.
Altogether, these data demonstrate that 5-HT
2A
